config.title: Lippincott Anatomy & Embryology Block 1
config.subtitle: General principles, early development, pelvis/perineum embryology, back, and upper limb anatomy

questions.stem: Which of the following is true of the anatomical position?
choices: The humerus is proximal to the scapula.
The radius is medial to the ulna.
The vertebral arch is ventral to the vertebral body.
The femur is superior to the fibula.
The phalanges of the foot are cranial to the metatarsals.
questions.explanation: In the anatomical position, the body stands erect facing forward with palms anterior; the thigh (femur) lies superior to the leg, so the femur is superior to the fibula. The humerus is distal (not proximal) to the scapula, hanging from its lateral corner. The radius lies lateral, not medial, to the ulna. The vertebral arch is dorsal, not ventral, to the vertebral body.
keypoints: ⭐ Anatomical position: standing erect, palms facing anterior, toes pointing anterior, feet together
The femur is superior to both the tibia and fibula in this position
Radius = lateral forearm bone; ulna = medial forearm bone
Vertebral arch (pedicles + laminae) sits posterior (dorsal) to the vertebral body

questions.stem: If the body were sectioned along a ___ plane, it would be divided into ___ portions.
questions.explanation: A horizontal (transverse/axial) plane lies perpendicular to both the median and coronal planes and divides the body into superior and inferior portions. A sagittal plane divides the body into right and left portions, not anterior/posterior or superior/inferior. A coronal (frontal) plane divides the body into anterior and posterior portions, not superior/inferior or right/left.
keypoints: ⭐ Horizontal (transverse/axial) plane → superior vs. inferior portions
Sagittal plane → right vs. left portions (median sagittal plane divides into equal halves)
Coronal (frontal) plane → anterior vs. posterior portions
All three planes are mutually perpendicular

questions.stem: Which of the following is true of a median plane of the hand?
choices: It becomes a horizontal plane when the hand is medially rotated 90 degrees.
It becomes a coronal plane when the brachium (upper arm) is laterally rotated 90 degrees and abducted 90 degrees.
It is the same as a frontal plane.
It remains a median plane regardless of limb or body position.
questions.explanation: All anatomical descriptions are relative to the standard anatomical position; regardless of how a limb or the body is actually postured, the observer mentally transposes it back to the anatomical position, so the median plane of the hand is always described as the median plane. A median plane runs longitudinally through the middle (third) digit and is anteroposterior, not mediolateral, and it is perpendicular (not identical) to the frontal plane.
keypoints: ⭐ Anatomical descriptions never change with actual limb position — always referenced to standard anatomical position
Median plane of the hand runs through the middle (3rd) digit
A median (sagittal) plane is perpendicular to a frontal (coronal) plane
This convention avoids confusion when limbs are rotated or flexed during exam or imaging

questions.stem: A radiologist wishes to image the body in a plane parallel to both scapulae. Which of the following choices best describes the desired sectioning?
questions.explanation: The scapulae lie flat across the back, and a plane running parallel to both of them is a frontal (coronal) plane, dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts. A horizontal section passes at right angles to both median and coronal planes (superior/inferior division), and a sagittal section runs parallel to the median plane (right/left division) — neither is parallel to the scapulae.
keypoints: ⭐ Frontal (coronal) plane = plane parallel to the coronal suture and scapulae; divides body anterior/posterior
Transverse section = section perpendicular to the long axis of a structure (not always equal to horizontal)
A horizontal section of the abdomen often cuts obliquely through coiled bowel loops
Useful memory: 'coronal' shares its root with the coronal suture of the skull, which runs side-to-side like the scapulae

questions.stem: A young boy uses his right hand to screw-in a new light bulb. Which of the following terms best describes the screw-home movement of his forearm?
questions.explanation: The screw-home (clockwise, right-handed) motion of driving a bulb into its socket occurs as the palm and forearm rotate laterally, moving the palm from posterior to anterior facing — this is supination. Pronation is the opposite movement (palm rotates medially) and would actually unscrew the bulb with the right hand, though it is the screw-home motion for the left hand. Flexion/abduction/adduction describe movements in different planes, not forearm rotation.
keypoints: ⭐ Supination: palm rotates to face anterior (as when holding a bowl of soup)
Pronation: palm rotates to face posterior
Right-hand screw-home motion = supination; left-hand screw-home motion = pronation
Supination/pronation occur at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, not the wrist

questions.stem: Bones are often classified according to their shape and/or developmental pattern. Which of the following choices is an example of a flat bone?
questions.explanation: The sternum, along with the bones of the calvaria, is a classic flat bone — subcutaneous, relatively thick, and commonly used for bone marrow collection. The humerus is a long bone with a medullary cavity; the hamate is a short (carpal) bone lacking a medullary cavity; the maxilla is an irregular bone; and the patella is a sesamoid bone formed within a tendon.
keypoints: ⭐ Flat bones: sternum and calvarial bones — subcutaneous, used for marrow biopsy (sternum, iliac crest)
Long bones (e.g., humerus) have a diaphysis with a medullary cavity
Short bones (e.g., carpals, tarsals) lack a medullary cavity
Sesamoid bones (e.g., patella) form within tendons to improve mechanical advantage at joints

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a cartilaginous joint?
questions.explanation: The intervertebral disc joints, along with the pubic symphysis, mental symphysis, and epiphyseal plates, are cartilaginous joints in which bones are united by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage. The humeroulnar and tibiotalar joints are synovial joints, and the middle radioulnar and cranial sutural joints are fibrous joints.
keypoints: ⭐ Cartilaginous joints: intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, mental symphysis, epiphyseal plates
Fibrous joints: sutures, interosseous membrane (middle radioulnar joint), syndesmoses
Synovial joints: most joints of the limbs (e.g., humeroulnar, tibiotalar) — have a joint cavity and synovial fluid
Cartilaginous joints allow limited movement but provide strong, shock-absorbing unions

questions.stem: Synovial joints allow free movement between their bony elements. They are classified into multiple subtypes according to the shape of the articulating surfaces and/or the degree of movement allowed. Which of the following synovial joint types permits multiaxial movement?
questions.explanation: Ball-and-socket joints, such as the hip and glenohumeral joints, allow multiaxial movement including flexion-extension, abduction-adduction, and medial-lateral rotation. Pivot joints (e.g., proximal radioulnar joint) allow only uniaxial rotation, hinge joints (e.g., humeroulnar joint) allow only uniaxial flexion-extension, and condyloid/saddle joints typically allow biaxial movement.
keypoints: ⭐ Ball-and-socket joints (hip, shoulder) = multiaxial, most mobile joint type
Hinge joints (elbow) and pivot joints (proximal radioulnar, atlantoaxial) = uniaxial
Condyloid (metacarpophalangeal) and saddle (carpometacarpal of thumb) joints = biaxial
Greater mobility (as in the shoulder) generally trades off with reduced joint stability

questions.stem: A physician delivers an intramuscular injection into the lateral aspect of the shoulder. Which of the following sequences describes the correct order of tissue layers pierced by the needle, passing from superficial to deep?
choices: Epidermis, dermis, superficial fascia, epimysium, deep fascia
Dermis, epidermis, superficial fascia, deep fascia, epimysium
Dermis, epidermis, superficial fascia, epimysium, deep fascia
Epidermis, dermis, superficial fascia, deep fascia, epimysium
Epidermis, superficial fascia, dermis, deep fascia, epimysium
questions.explanation: From superficial to deep, a needle passes through the epidermis, the dermis, the superficial fascia (fatty subcutaneous tissue), the deep fascia (dense fat-free connective tissue), and finally the epimysium investing the muscle. Any sequence placing the dermis superficial to the epidermis, or the epimysium superficial to the deep fascia, is incorrect.
keypoints: ⭐ Correct order: epidermis → dermis → superficial fascia → deep fascia → epimysium → muscle
Superficial fascia = subcutaneous fat (loose connective tissue)
Deep fascia = dense, fat-free connective tissue layer investing muscle groups
Epimysium is a deep extension of deep fascia tightly wrapping an individual muscle

questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student on spring break suffers a first-degree sunburn on her back and upper limbs. Which of the following integumentary structures/functions is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: First-degree burns are superficial injuries limited to the epidermis, where many general sensory (pain) nerve endings terminate, accounting for the pain of sunburn. Hair follicles and subcutaneous fat lie deeper and are typically spared in first-degree burns; the skin produces vitamin D, not vitamin A; and parasympathetic fibers are not distributed to the body wall/limb skin at all.
keypoints: ⭐ First-degree burns damage only the epidermis (e.g., typical sunburn)
Second-degree burns extend into superficial dermis; third-degree burns are full-thickness
General sensory (GSA) nerve endings penetrate into the epidermis and mediate burn pain
Skin synthesizes vitamin D, not vitamin A

questions.stem: A teenage boy breaks a pane of glass with his fist and receives a laceration to the posterior aspect of his wrist. He notices the tendons that cross his wrist lift out of place (or bowstring) when he extends his wrist. Which of the following structures was most likely cut by the broken glass?
questions.explanation: A retinaculum is a thickened band of deep fascia that holds tendons in place as they cross a joint, preventing them from bowstringing during joint movement; its disruption explains the tendon lift-off. A bursa and synovial tendon sheath reduce friction but do not anchor tendons in place, and an intermuscular septum separates muscle compartments rather than restraining crossing tendons.
keypoints: ⭐ Retinacula (e.g., extensor/flexor retinaculum of the wrist) prevent tendon bowstringing across joints
Bursae are fluid-filled sacs that reduce friction between structures, not tendon restraints
Synovial tendon sheaths are elongated bursae enclosing tendons, common at the wrist and ankle
Intermuscular septa organize muscles into osseofascial compartments

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy engages in an intensive weight-lifting program to build muscle strength. The growth of his muscles is the result of which of the following processes?
questions.explanation: Postnatal muscle growth from resistance exercise results from hypertrophy — an increase in the size (and number of myofibrils) of existing muscle fibers — rather than the creation of new fibers. Hyperplasia (an increase in fiber number) is not the normal mechanism of exercise-induced growth in adults, and atrophy describes muscle wasting, the opposite process.
keypoints: ⭐ Skeletal muscle growth with exercise = hypertrophy (increased fiber size), not hyperplasia
Limited hyperplasia can occur postnatally via satellite cells after muscle trauma/degeneration
Atrophy = muscle wasting, often from denervation or disuse
Muscle tonus is baseline partial contraction, unrelated to strength training gains

questions.stem: Which of the following structures are innervated by somatic motor neurons?
choices: Arrector pili muscles of hair follicles
questions.explanation: Somatic motor (general somatic efferent) neurons innervate skeletal muscle derived from embryonic myotomes, such as the semispinalis muscle of the back. Meissner corpuscles carry general sensory (afferent) information, while arrector pili muscles, cardiac muscle, and vascular smooth muscle are all innervated by visceral motor (autonomic) neurons, not somatic motor neurons.
keypoints: ⭐ Somatic motor (GSE) neurons supply only skeletal muscle derived from myotomes
Smooth muscle (arrector pili, vessel walls) and cardiac muscle are innervated by autonomic (GVE) neurons
Meissner corpuscles are sensory receptors, carrying GSA fibers, not motor
Five functional nerve fiber components: GSA, GVA, GVE, GSE, and special sensory

questions.stem: A man exhibits anhydrosis (lack of sweating) and erythema (flushing) on his chest due to loss of sympathetic innervation. A thorough neurological analysis reveals dysfunction of presynaptic (preganglionic) sympathetic nerve cell bodies. Which of the following sites is most likely damaged in this patient?
choices: Lateral gray horn of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Presynaptic sympathetic neuron cell bodies reside in the lateral gray horn of the spinal cord at levels T1 through L2/L3, giving the sympathetic division its thoracolumbar outflow. The brainstem houses presynaptic parasympathetic neurons (craniosacral outflow); the sympathetic chain and prevertebral ganglia contain postsynaptic sympathetic cell bodies; and dorsal root ganglia house sensory, not motor, neuron cell bodies.
keypoints: ⭐ Presynaptic sympathetic cell bodies: lateral gray horn, spinal levels T1–L2/L3 (thoracolumbar outflow)
Presynaptic parasympathetic cell bodies: brainstem nuclei (CN III, VII, IX, X) and sacral cord S2-4 (craniosacral outflow)
Postsynaptic sympathetic cell bodies: sympathetic chain ganglia (limbs/body wall) and prevertebral ganglia (abdominopelvic viscera)
Dorsal root ganglia contain pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies only

questions.stem: A research scientist at a pharmaceutical company discovers a new drug that selectively blocks the release of norepinephrine from nerve endings. At which of the following sites would this drug have the greatest effect on normal synaptic transmission?
choices: Synapses between presynaptic and postsynaptic parasympathetic neurons
Synapses between presynaptic and postsynaptic sympathetic neurons
questions.explanation: Postsynaptic sympathetic neurons are noradrenergic, releasing norepinephrine at their terminals (with the notable exception of sweat glands, which receive cholinergic postsynaptic sympathetic fibers), so a norepinephrine-release blocker would most affect these terminals. Somatic motor end plates and all pre-to-postganglionic autonomic synapses use acetylcholine, as do postsynaptic parasympathetic terminals.
keypoints: ⭐ Postsynaptic sympathetic terminals are noradrenergic (release norepinephrine) — main exception: sweat glands (cholinergic)
All autonomic ganglionic synapses (pre-to-postsynaptic) use acetylcholine, in both divisions
Postsynaptic parasympathetic terminals and somatic motor end plates are cholinergic
This distinction underlies selectivity of many autonomic and sympathomimetic/lytic drugs

questions.stem: A young couple hoping for a pregnancy buys an over-the-counter pregnancy kit. What substance will this test most likely detect?
questions.explanation: Over-the-counter pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a glycoprotein produced by the syncytiotrophoblast that maintains the corpus luteum; it is detectable in urine after implantation. Early pregnancy factor appears earlier (24–48 hours post-fertilization) but requires costly detection methods not used in home kits. Progesterone and estrogen support pregnancy but are not used as detection markers, and LH surges before ovulation rather than signaling pregnancy.
keypoints: ⭐ Home pregnancy tests detect urinary hCG, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast
hCG maintains the corpus luteum, sustaining progesterone production until the placenta takes over
hCG is not detectable until after implantation (~6–12 days post-fertilization), risking false negatives if tested too early
Early pregnancy factor (EPF) appears earlier but is not practical for over-the-counter testing

questions.stem: The given illustration depicts the passage of a human egg through the female reproductive tract from ovulation to implantation. These events occur during the 1st week of development. Fertilization normally occurs at which of the indicated steps?
choices: Ampullary region of the uterine tube
questions.explanation: Fertilization normally occurs in the ampullary region of the uterine tube, the expanded distal segment near the ovary, where sperm (after capacitation and the acrosome reaction) meet the oocyte. At the preovulatory and immediate postovulation stages the oocyte is not yet accessible for fertilization, and the 2-cell and blastocyst stages represent post-fertilization development as the zygote travels toward and implants in the uterus.
keypoints: ⭐ Fertilization site: ampulla of the uterine tube
Sperm must undergo capacitation and the acrosome reaction before fertilizing the oocyte
The zygote reaches the uterine cavity as a 16-cell morula ~3–4 days after fertilization
By ~4.5 days the conceptus is an early blastocyst; the zona pellucida disappears just before implantation
questions.imageAlt: Diagram of the female reproductive tract showing ovulation, fertilization, and transport of the egg to the uterus
questions.imageCaption: Passage of the oocyte from ovary to implantation during week 1 of development

questions.stem: A 43-year-old pregnant woman at 16 weeks of gestation comes to her OB/GYN for a normal examination. During routine blood tests, her serum a-fetoprotein (AFP) concentration is markedly decreased for her gestational age. Which abnormality or condition will the physician need to rule out based upon these low AFP levels?
questions.explanation: Decreased maternal serum AFP is associated with chromosomal defects such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21) and trisomy 18, warranting further workup (e.g., amniocentesis). Spina bifida and anencephaly are neural tube defects that raise (not lower) AFP because of exposed neural tissue leaking AFP into the amniotic fluid; multifetal pregnancy and hepatocellular carcinoma likewise elevate, rather than decrease, AFP.
keypoints: ⭐ Decreased maternal serum AFP → chromosomal abnormalities (Down syndrome, trisomy 18)
Increased maternal serum AFP → neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly), abdominal wall defects, multifetal pregnancy
AFP is produced by the fetal liver and yolk sac and crosses into maternal blood
Maternal age over 35 increases risk of fetal chromosomal abnormalities

questions.stem: Which structure is derived from the same embryonic primordia as the spinal (posterior root) ganglia?
questions.explanation: Both the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia and the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla arise from neural crest cells. The kidney arises from intermediate mesoderm, the liver and lungs from endodermal gut tube outgrowths, and the vertebrae from the sclerotome portion of paraxial mesoderm-derived somites — none of which are neural crest derivatives.
keypoints: ⭐ Neural crest derivatives: dorsal root ganglia, adrenal medulla, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, thyroid C cells
Kidney and gonads arise from intermediate mesoderm
Liver and lungs arise as endodermal outgrowths of the foregut
Vertebrae arise from sclerotome (paraxial mesoderm-derived somites)

questions.stem: The given illustration shows a dorsal view of a human embryo. In the embryo, neurulation is well underway, and several distinct somites are present on each side of the neural tube. The development of the embryo depicted in this illustration is typical of which of the following embryonic periods?
questions.explanation: Most of neurulation (neural tube formation), substantial somite differentiation, and early pharyngeal arch/limb bud appearance occur during week 4; an embryo with near-complete neural tube closure and numerous defined somites is characteristic of this stage. Week 3 features gastrulation and trilaminar disc formation (only beginning neurulation), week 1–2 predate germ layer/neural tube formation entirely, and by week 5 limb buds and pharyngeal arches are already well developed beyond what is shown.
keypoints: ⭐ Week 3 = gastrulation, trilaminar germ disc ('threes' for 3 germ layers)
Week 4 = neurulation completes, somite differentiation, pharyngeal arches and upper limb bud appear
Somite number is used to accurately stage embryos between weeks 3–5 (~3 pairs added per day)
Weeks 3–8 constitute the embryonic (organogenesis) period, most sensitive to teratogens

questions.stem: A male newborn suffers a complex of congenital defects involving malformation of the urinary and genital ducts. Examination of his family history reveals several members sharing a similar background of urinary and genital problems spanning three generations. These issues may be related to a genetic defect that is expressed in which of the following embryonic sites?
questions.explanation: The urinary and genital systems both develop from the intermediate mesoderm, which forms the urogenital ridge giving rise to the excretory organs, gonads, and genital duct system, so heritable defects in this region manifest as combined urogenital malformations. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites (muscle, dermis, axial skeleton); neural crest forms diverse structures including ganglia and pigment cells; surface ectoderm forms skin and its appendages; and yolk sac endoderm largely forms the gut lining.
keypoints: ⭐ Intermediate mesoderm → urogenital ridge → kidneys, gonads, genital ducts
Paraxial mesoderm → somites → sclerotome, dermatome, myotome
Neural crest → autonomic/sensory ganglia, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, pharyngeal skeleton
Primordial germ cells originate in the epiblast, migrate through the yolk sac wall, then colonize the genital ridges

questions.stem: In a 15-day embryo, the epiblast is capable of forming which of the following germ layers?
questions.explanation: During gastrulation, epiblast cells that invaginate through the primitive streak displace the hypoblast to form definitive endoderm and also generate the intraembryonic mesoderm, while epiblast cells that do not migrate remain to form the ectoderm — so the epiblast is the source of all three germ layers. Any answer omitting one of the three layers misses part of this process, since endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm all trace back to epiblast-derived cells.
keypoints: ⭐ The epiblast is the sole source of all three germ layers via gastrulation
Invaginating epiblast cells at the primitive streak displace the hypoblast to become definitive endoderm
Migrating epiblast cells that remain between the germ layers become intraembryonic mesoderm
Non-migrating epiblast cells that stay on the dorsal surface become ectoderm

questions.stem: The given illustration represents a lateral view of an approximately 25-day-old human embryo. Disruption of further development of the structures indicated by the "X" could directly affect the formation of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: The structures marked "X" are somites, derived from paraxial mesoderm, whose myotome portion splits into an epimere (intrinsic back muscles) and hypomere (anterolateral body wall and limb muscles) — so somite disruption would impair skeletal muscle formation in the arm. Limb bones and dermis instead arise from lateral plate (somatic) mesoderm, body hair and melanocytes derive from ectoderm/neural crest, and intestinal lining derives from endoderm.
keypoints: ⭐ Somites (paraxial mesoderm) → myotome (skeletal muscle), dermatome (dermis), sclerotome (axial skeleton)
Myotome splits into epimere (back muscles) and hypomere (limb and body wall muscles)
Limb bones arise from lateral plate (somatic) mesoderm, not somites
Melanocytes are neural crest derivatives; gut lining is endoderm-derived
questions.imageAlt: Lateral view diagram of a 25-day human embryo with somites and pharyngeal arches labeled, X marking the somites
questions.imageCaption: Lateral view of a 25-day embryo; X indicates the somites

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who does not know that she is pregnant undergoes a chemotherapy treatment at the end of her 1st week of pregnancy. Chemotherapy is associated with slowing the rate of mitosis in exposed cells. In which of the following layers would a lowered rate of cell division be most likely to hinder implantation of the blastocyst?
questions.explanation: The cytotrophoblast is the mitotically active inner layer of the trophoblast that forms primary chorionic villi and supplies cells that migrate into and expand the syncytiotrophoblast, so slowed mitosis here would directly impair implantation. The syncytiotrophoblast itself is mitotically inactive and depends on cytotrophoblast input; the amnioblast, epiblast, and hypoblast contribute to the embryo proper and amnion but are not the drivers of trophoblastic invasion.
keypoints: ⭐ Cytotrophoblast is the mitotically active layer that drives trophoblast/placental expansion
Syncytiotrophoblast is multinucleated, mitotically inactive, and erodes the endometrium
Epiblast/hypoblast form the bilaminar disc (embryo proper), not the implanting trophoblast
Chemotherapy's antimitotic effect can impair implantation by targeting rapidly dividing cytotrophoblast

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman is surprised to discover that she is pregnant. Following a review of her menstrual history and sexual activity, her physician determines that she is in the 4th week of pregnancy. Which of the following best describes the condition of the embryo at this time?
choices: Gastrulation is complete, resulting in two germ layers
The embryo is entering a period of relative resistance to teratogenic substances
The trophoblast is present, but the syncytiotrophoblast has not yet formed
questions.explanation: By the end of week 4, neurulation (which begins late in week 3) is nearly complete, along with substantial somite differentiation and the appearance of the pharyngeal arches and upper limb bud. Gastrulation (week 3) produces three, not two, germ layers; weeks 3–8 are the most teratogen-sensitive period, not resistant; somites are well underway by week 4; and the syncytiotrophoblast differentiates from the trophoblast early in week 2.
keypoints: ⭐ Week 4: neurulation nearly complete, ~26–29 somite pairs, pharyngeal arches and upper limb bud appear
Week 3 = gastrulation, forming all three germ layers (not two)
Weeks 3–8 are the most teratogen-sensitive ('critical') period of development, not resistant
Trophoblast differentiates into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast early in week 2

questions.stem: A 4-month-old male infant presents with a "growing sore" located posterior to his left ear. This sore is diagnosed as a postauricular hemangioma, as seen in the given photo with the auricle pulled anterior. The cells forming the hemangioma are derived from which of the following cell layers?
questions.explanation: Hemangiomas are vascular tumors composed of proliferating blood vessels and vascular endothelium, both mesodermal derivatives (mesoderm gives rise to blood cells, vascular endothelium, connective tissue, and muscle). Endoderm forms gut and glandular epithelium, neural crest forms ganglia/pigment/pharyngeal skeletal elements, neuroectoderm forms CNS neurons and glia, and ectoderm forms epidermis and its appendages — none of which produce vascular endothelium.
keypoints: ⭐ Hemangiomas are mesodermal in origin (angioblasts/vascular endothelium, blood cells)
Mesoderm derivatives: muscle, connective tissue, bone, cartilage, blood, dermis, kidney, spleen, gonads
Neural crest derivatives include Schwann cells, ganglia, melanocytes, pharyngeal skeletal elements — not vessels
Postauricular hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors of infancy, often regressing spontaneously
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photo of a postauricular hemangioma behind the left ear of an infant, with the auricle pulled forward
questions.imageCaption: Postauricular hemangioma in a 4-month-old infant

questions.stem: The notochord forms the initial axial skeletal element of the body and induces the formation of the neural plate. Which of the following structures is the sole postnatal remnant of the embryonic notochord?
questions.explanation: The notochord is almost entirely replaced by sclerotomal cells forming the vertebral bodies, but its central core persists as the nucleus pulposus, the hydrostatic core of each intervertebral disc (the structure that herniates in a 'slipped disc'). The spinal cord derives from the neural tube (induced by, but not made from, the notochord); the rib cage and anulus fibrosus derive from sclerotome; and the meninges derive from mesoderm (dura) and neural crest (arachnoid/pia).
keypoints: ⭐ Nucleus pulposus = the only postnatal remnant of the notochord
Notochord induces neural plate formation but is itself replaced by sclerotome-derived vertebral bodies
Anulus fibrosus (surrounding the nucleus pulposus) is sclerotome-derived, not notochord-derived
Disc herniation involves the nucleus pulposus protruding through a weakened anulus fibrosus

questions.stem: A 22-year-old pregnant woman at 20 weeks of gestation comes to her OB/GYN for a scheduled prenatal examination. Routine blood tests indicate that her serum a-fetoprotein (AFP) concentration is markedly increased for her gestational age. Ultrasonography reveals a lower lumbar spina bifida in the fetus. During which weeks of gestation did this defect most likely occur?
questions.explanation: Neurulation begins late in week 3, and the posterior neuropore normally closes around day 27 (week 4); failure of this closure produces lower neural tube defects such as spina bifida, so the defect arises during weeks 4–6. Weeks 1–2 precede neurulation entirely, and weeks 9 and beyond occur well after neural tube closure is normally complete, making them too late for the primary defect to originate.
keypoints: ⭐ Posterior neuropore closes ~day 27 (week 4); failure causes lower neural tube defects (spina bifida)
Anterior neuropore closes ~day 25; failure causes anencephaly or cranial defects
Neural tube defects are associated with elevated maternal serum and amniotic fluid AFP
Folic acid supplementation before/during early pregnancy reduces neural tube defect risk

questions.stem: A male infant presents with prune belly syndrome, as shown in the given photo. In this syndrome, the abdominal wall musculature is poorly developed, resulting in an abdominal wall so thin that the internal organs are visible and easily palpable. The muscles affected in this condition develop from which of the following embryonic sites?
questions.explanation: The hypomere, the ventral portion of the myotome, gives rise to muscles of the anterolateral body wall (including the abdominal wall) and limbs, so its maldevelopment underlies the deficient abdominal musculature of prune belly syndrome. The epimere instead forms the intrinsic back muscles; intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital system (though prune belly syndrome also often features urinary anomalies, the muscle deficiency itself is hypomere-derived); splanchnic mesoderm forms cardiac/gut smooth muscle; and ectoderm does not form skeletal muscle.
keypoints: ⭐ Hypomere → anterolateral body wall and limb skeletal muscles (ventral primary rami innervate)
Epimere → intrinsic back muscles (dorsal primary rami innervate)
Prune belly (Eagle-Barrett) syndrome often also involves urinary tract anomalies and cryptorchidism
Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm forms cardiac muscle and gut tube smooth muscle, not body wall skeletal muscle
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photo of an infant with prune belly syndrome showing a thin, wrinkled abdominal wall with visible underlying organs
questions.imageCaption: Infant with prune belly (Eagle-Barrett) syndrome

questions.stem: Which structure is derived from the same embryonic primordium as the kidney?
questions.explanation: Both the kidneys and gonads develop from the intermediate mesoderm, which forms the urogenital ridge. The epidermis arises from ectoderm, the pineal gland from neuroectoderm, the liver from lateral plate (splanchnic) mesoderm/endoderm interaction, and the adrenal medulla from neural crest — none sharing the intermediate mesoderm origin of the kidney.
keypoints: ⭐ Kidney and gonad share a common origin: intermediate mesoderm (urogenital ridge)
Adrenal cortex is also mesodermal (from the same ridge region), but adrenal medulla is neural crest-derived
Liver develops from an endodermal foregut outgrowth invading splanchnic mesoderm (septum transversum)
Pineal gland is a neuroectodermal derivative of the diencephalon

questions.stem: A developmental neurobiologist surgically removes the neural crest in the thoracic region of a chicken embryo immediately after closure of the neural tube. Which of the following cell types is most likely to be affected?
choices: Autonomic ganglia in the thoracic cavity
Epithelial cells lining the lower respiratory tract
Skeletal muscle cells in the thoracic wall
questions.explanation: All autonomic ganglia (along with dorsal root ganglia) are neural crest derivatives, so removing the thoracic neural crest would prevent formation of thoracic autonomic ganglia. Cardiac muscle arises from splanchnic mesoderm, lower respiratory epithelium from endoderm, and rib bone and thoracic skeletal muscle from paraxial mesoderm (sclerotome and myotome, respectively) — none dependent on neural crest.
keypoints: ⭐ Neural crest gives rise to all autonomic ganglia and dorsal root ganglia
Other neural crest derivatives: Schwann cells, meninges (arachnoid/pia), melanocytes, adrenal medulla, thyroid C cells, pharyngeal arch skeleton
Cardiac muscle = splanchnic mesoderm; rib/thoracic wall muscle = paraxial mesoderm (sclerotome/myotome)
Lower respiratory tract epithelium = endoderm (from the respiratory diverticulum of the foregut)

questions.stem: A married couple having difficulty with conception keeps a daily diary of the female's basal body temperature (BBT). On Friday, the woman noted a slight elevation in her BBT, which may indicate that she is ovulating. If her ovum is expelled into the peritoneal cavity from the ovary (ovulation), the secondary oocyte resides at what specific stage of meiosis?
choices: Meiosis is completed at the time of ovulation
questions.explanation: At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase of meiosis II and remains there until (unless) fertilization occurs. Primary oocytes, not secondary oocytes, are the ones dormant in prophase of meiosis I before puberty; metaphase I is completed before ovulation (producing the secondary oocyte and first polar body); and meiosis is only completed after fertilization triggers resumption of meiosis II.
keypoints: ⭐ Ovulated secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase of meiosis II until fertilization
Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of meiosis I from fetal life until stimulated after puberty
Meiosis I yields the secondary oocyte plus the first polar body just before ovulation
If fertilization does not occur, the secondary oocyte degenerates ~24 hours after ovulation
questions.imageAlt: Diagram of oogenesis showing the stages of oocyte maturation from primary oocyte through ovulation
questions.imageCaption: Stages of oogenesis and meiotic arrest at ovulation

questions.stem: The amniotic cavity forms during the process of implantation of the blastocyst. The amniotic cavity forms within which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Small spaces develop between epiblast cells and coalesce into the amniotic cavity, which is therefore lined by epiblast (amnioblast) cells on the dorsal aspect of the bilaminar disc. The hypoblast instead lines the primitive yolk sac ventrally; the cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast form the trophoblastic (placental) layers; and the maternal endometrium is the site of implantation, not the source of the amniotic cavity.
keypoints: ⭐ Amniotic cavity forms within the epiblast and is lined by epiblast (amnioblast) cells
Hypoblast lines the primitive yolk sac (exocoelomic cavity), located ventral to the bilaminar disc
Bilaminar germ disc = epiblast (dorsal) + hypoblast (ventral), each bordering its own cavity
The amnion expands to eventually surround the entire fetus by the end of the embryonic period

questions.stem: A married woman who is having difficulty getting pregnant undergoes an endometrial function test (EFT), which determines that the endometrium of her uterus is not capable of implantation. Which of the following substances would likely increase the chances for implantation of the fertilized oocyte (or preimplantation embryo) into the uterine mucosa?
questions.explanation: Progesterone, produced by the corpus luteum after ovulation, halts endometrial proliferation and transforms the endometrium into a secretory, receptive state for implantation, so supplementation would improve implantation chances. FSH and LH act earlier to drive follicular maturation and ovulation rather than endometrial receptivity; estrogen proliferates the endometrium but does not prepare it for implantation the way progesterone does; and testosterone has minimal physiologic effect on the female endometrium.
keypoints: ⭐ Progesterone (from the corpus luteum) converts a proliferative endometrium into a secretory, implantation-ready state
Estrogen drives endometrial proliferation but progesterone is required for implantation receptivity
FSH and LH act on the ovary (follicle maturation and ovulation), not directly on endometrial receptivity
Luteal phase progesterone insufficiency is a recognized cause of implantation failure/infertility

questions.stem: Development of the primitive gonads into testes or ovaries is induced by invasion of the genital ridges by the primordial germ cells. These cells migrate from which of the following locations?
questions.explanation: Primordial germ cells originate in the epiblast and migrate to the caudal endodermal wall of the yolk sac (near the allantois), then travel along the dorsal mesentery of the gut tube to reach and invade the genital ridges, inducing gonadal differentiation. Intermediate mesoderm is the destination (forming the genital ridge itself), not the source, of these cells, while paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm and neural crest give rise to unrelated structures (somites, body wall/gut wall, and pigment/ganglion cells, respectively).
keypoints: ⭐ Primordial germ cells arise in the epiblast, transiently reside in the yolk sac wall, then migrate via the dorsal mesentery to the genital ridges
Intermediate mesoderm forms the genital ridge/urogenital structures that the germ cells invade — not their origin
Failure of germ cell migration can result in gonadal dysgenesis
The genital ridge cannot differentiate into a testis or ovary without primordial germ cell invasion

questions.stem: The urinary system develops from which of the embryonic sources labeled in the given diagram?
questions.explanation: The urinary system (kidney parenchyma, nephrons) develops from the intermediate mesoderm, the small bridge of mesoderm connecting the paraxial mesoderm to the lateral plate mesoderm. Paraxial mesoderm instead forms somites (muscle, dermis, vertebral column); parietal (somatic) and visceral (splanchnic) lateral plate mesoderm form the body wall/limbs and gut tube wall, respectively; and yolk sac endoderm forms the gut tube lining.
keypoints: ⭐ Intermediate mesoderm → kidney parenchyma, nephrons, and gonads (via the urogenital ridge)
Paraxial mesoderm → somites → myotome/dermatome/sclerotome
Lateral plate mesoderm splits into parietal (body wall) and visceral (gut wall) layers
Yolk sac endoderm contributes the epithelial lining of the gut tube, not the urinary system
questions.imageAlt: Cross-sectional diagram of an embryo labeling the germ layer/mesoderm subdivisions A through E
questions.imageCaption: Embryonic mesoderm subdivisions; intermediate mesoderm (labeled B) gives rise to the urinary system

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man experiences severe lower back pain for 4 days after moving heavy furniture. After a thorough back evaluation and review of associated radiological imaging, a surgeon removes the herniated portion of the L3-4 intervertebral (IV) disc. What type of cartilage most likely gives the tensile strength of the disc extracted from this patient?
questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage (fibrous cartilage), rich in Type I collagen, forms the tough anulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc and provides its tensile strength; hyperflexion can tear it, allowing the nucleus pulposus to herniate posteriorly. Hyaline cartilage instead covers articular surfaces and forms the epiphyseal growth plate template, elastic cartilage provides flexible support in structures like the ear and epiglottis, and 'anular' is not a true cartilage type (anular/cricoid cartilage is a laryngeal structure, not a tissue type).
keypoints: ⭐ Fibrocartilage (Type I collagen) provides the anulus fibrosus's tensile strength
Hyaline cartilage (Type II collagen) covers joint surfaces and forms the epiphyseal plate template
Elastic cartilage supports flexible structures: external ear, auditory tube, epiglottis
Disc herniation occurs when the anulus fibrosus tears, allowing nucleus pulposus to protrude posteriorly

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man goes to his family physician complaining of lower back pain. During examination, the doctor notes a tuft of hair and a dimple on the skin of the patient's lower back. A plain film reveals a congenital defect in his L5 vertebra, indicated by the black arrow in the given X-ray. No other structural abnormalities are noted. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation: Spina bifida occulta is the mildest neural tube defect, in which the neural arches fail to fuse dorsally but the split is too small for meninges or cord to protrude; it is often marked only by a hair tuft, dimple, or birthmark and is typically asymptomatic, as seen on this X-ray showing an isolated lamina defect at L5. Meningocele and the cystica/myeloschisis forms all present with a protruding cyst-like sac (absent here), and anencephaly is a lethal cranial defect incompatible with reaching 45 years of age.
keypoints: ⭐ Spina bifida occulta: isolated failure of neural arch fusion, no protrusion, often with overlying hair tuft/dimple
Present in ~10% of the general population, usually asymptomatic and unrelated to back pain
Meningocele = meninges protrude into a CSF-filled sac; spinal cord stays in normal position
Meningomyelocele (most common spina bifida cystica) = meninges + spinal cord protrude into the sac
questions.imageAlt: Plain film X-ray of the lumbosacral spine with an arrow indicating a laminar defect at L5
questions.imageCaption: Plain film showing a congenital defect (failure of laminar fusion) at L5

questions.stem: A developmental biologist studying the derivatives of the somites and somitomeres treats the epimeres in a mouse embryo with a toxin that kills all of their cells. If the mouse develops to full term, which of the following muscles is most likely to be absent?
questions.explanation: The longissimus, one of the erector spinae muscles, is derived from the epimere (the dorsal portion of the myotome) and thus would be absent if epimeres were destroyed. The latissimus dorsi, rhomboid major, and levator scapulae are hypomere-derived superficial back muscles innervated by ventral primary rami, and the trapezius is a pharyngeal arch/branchiomeric-derived muscle innervated by the accessory nerve (CN XI), unrelated to either myotome subdivision.
keypoints: ⭐ Epimere → intrinsic (deep) back muscles: erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis), transversospinales, innervated by dorsal primary rami
Hypomere → superficial extrinsic back muscles (latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae) that act on the limb, innervated by ventral primary rami
Trapezius and sternocleidomastoid are NOT myotome derivatives — innervated by CN XI (accessory nerve)
Deep back muscles are also called epaxial muscles; superficial limb-related back muscles are hypaxial

questions.stem: A lesion of which of the indicated structures would cause loss of sensation in the skin overlying the trapezius muscle?
choices: Lateral gray horn of spinal cord
questions.explanation: General sensory fibers from the skin overlying the trapezius travel via the posterior (dorsal) primary rami of spinal nerves to the posterior gray horn, so a lesion here causes loss of sensation over the back. The lateral gray horn houses presynaptic sympathetic neurons (autonomic, not cutaneous sensory); the anterior root and anterior primary ramus carry motor fibers and sensory fibers from the anterolateral body wall/limbs (not the back skin); and the sympathetic trunk carries autonomic and visceral sensory fibers unrelated to back skin sensation.
keypoints: ⭐ Skin overlying the back (including over the trapezius) is innervated by posterior (dorsal) primary rami
Trapezius muscle itself is supplied by CN XI (accessory nerve), not by rami of spinal nerves
Anterior primary rami supply the skin of the anterolateral trunk and limbs, not the back
Posterior primary rami also carry motor fibers to the deep (epaxial) back muscles
questions.imageAlt: Cross-sectional diagram of a spinal nerve and spinal cord with structures labeled A through E
questions.imageCaption: Spinal nerve/spinal cord cross section; E indicates the posterior (dorsal) primary ramus

questions.stem: An infant suffers a vertebral malformation in which the nucleus pulposus component of multiple intervertebral discs is hypertrophied. From what embryonic structure is the hypertrophied structure derived?
questions.explanation: The nucleus pulposus is the sole postnatal remnant of the embryonic notochord, which is otherwise replaced by sclerotome-derived vertebral bodies. The dermatome forms dermis, the myotome forms skeletal muscle (via epimere/hypomere), the sclerotome forms the vertebrae and anulus fibrosus (not the nucleus pulposus), and neural crest forms ganglia rather than disc tissue.
keypoints: ⭐ Nucleus pulposus = notochord remnant; anulus fibrosus = sclerotome-derived
Notochord induces neural plate formation before being replaced by vertebral bodies
Sclerotome, dermatome, and myotome are the three somite derivatives
Nucleus pulposus herniation ('slipped disc') reflects its distinct notochordal, gelatinous composition

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man's car is struck from behind by a truck, causing a severe hyperextension neck injury. The given T2-weighted MRI shows a rupture of the anterior anulus of the C4-5 intervertebral disc, inflammation of that disc, and a prevertebral hematoma. Which of the following ligaments is disrupted in this injury?
questions.explanation: The anterior longitudinal ligament runs along the anterior vertebral bodies and resists hyperextension; the extreme hyperextension forces in this rear-end collision overpowered and ruptured it, seen as an abnormal hyperintense signal anterior to C5 on MRI. The posterior longitudinal ligament resists flexion (not hyperextension) and lies posteriorly; the ligamentum flavum and interspinous ligament also resist flexion; and the intertransverse ligament resists contralateral bending, none of which are the primary structures stressed by hyperextension.
keypoints: ⭐ Anterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperextension of the vertebral column
Posterior longitudinal ligament, ligamentum flavum, and interspinous ligament resist flexion
Whiplash (hyperextension) injuries classically damage the anterior longitudinal ligament and anterior anulus fibrosus
MRI shows ligament disruption as an interruption in the normal hypointense (dark) ligament band
questions.imageAlt: T2-weighted sagittal cervical MRI showing anterior longitudinal ligament disruption and C4-5 disc injury
questions.imageCaption: Sagittal cervical MRI showing anterior longitudinal ligament rupture at C4-5

questions.stem: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; Lou Gehrig's disease) is a progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease caused by degeneration of the motor neurons controlling skeletal (voluntary) muscle movement. Postmortem analysis of which of the following structures would show the cell bodies of neurons affected by this disease?
choices: Anterior gray horn of the spinal cord
Lateral gray horn of the spinal cord
Posterior gray horn of the spinal cord
Lateral column of spinal cord white matter
questions.explanation: Somatic motor (alpha motor) neuron cell bodies supplying skeletal muscle reside in the anterior (ventral) gray horn of the spinal cord at every segmental level, and these are the neurons destroyed in ALS. The lateral gray horn houses autonomic (sympathetic) neurons, the posterior gray horn contains interneurons receiving sensory input, spinal ganglia house sensory neuron cell bodies, and white matter columns contain axons and glia rather than motor neuron cell bodies.
keypoints: ⭐ ALS destroys somatic motor neurons in the anterior (ventral) gray horn (and corticospinal tract upper motor neurons)
Lateral gray horn (T1-L2/3) = presynaptic sympathetic neurons, not somatic motor
Posterior gray horn = sensory interneurons receiving primary afferent input
Spinal ganglia = sensory (afferent) neuron cell bodies, spared in ALS

questions.stem: A 19-year-old girl gives birth to a baby girl diagnosed with a meningomyelocele, as seen in the given midsagittal MRI. The mother lived in a rural area and did not have prenatal visits with her obstetrician. Which of the following drugs, if taken in the proper doses during the periconceptional period, would have greatly reduced the chances of her fetus having a neural tube defect (NTD)?
questions.explanation: Periconceptional folic acid (vitamin B9) supplementation reduces the incidence of neural tube defects by up to 70%, since neural tube closure occurs within the first 28 days after conception, often before pregnancy is recognized. Valproic acid is itself a known teratogen that increases NTD risk, while cephalexin, acetaminophen, and famotidine are not protective folate supplements and are not established NTD-prevention agents.
keypoints: ⭐ Periconceptional folic acid supplementation reduces NTD incidence by up to ~70%
Recommended: 400 mcg folic acid daily beginning ~3 months before conception, continued through pregnancy
Valproic acid (an anticonvulsant) is a known teratogen that increases NTD risk
Neural tube closure is complete by ~day 28, often before a woman knows she is pregnant
questions.imageAlt: Midsagittal MRI of a newborn showing a meningomyelocele in the lower spine
questions.imageCaption: Midsagittal MRI showing a meningomyelocele

questions.stem: An internal medicine attending physician asks a medical student to place the bell of her stethoscope on the triangle of auscultation to hear a patient's breathing sounds. Which of the following structures make up the boundaries of this triangle?
choices: Latissimus dorsi, ilium, external abdominal oblique
questions.explanation: The triangle of auscultation is bounded by the lateral edge of the trapezius, the medial border of the scapula, and the upper edge of the latissimus dorsi; this gap in the muscular layers overlies the posterior chest wall, making it ideal for hearing lung sounds. The deltoid/latissimus/scapula grouping instead outlines the posterior axilla, and the other listed groupings define the lumbar triangle or neck/back regions unrelated to lung auscultation.
keypoints: ⭐ Triangle of auscultation: trapezius (medial), scapula (lateral), latissimus dorsi (inferior)
This gap in muscle coverage overlies lung tissue, optimal for auscultating breath sounds
Lumbar (Petit) triangle: latissimus dorsi, iliac crest, external oblique — a site of potential hernia
Distinct from the posterior axilla, bounded by deltoid, latissimus dorsi, and scapula

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man fell 25 ft, landing on his back. The given sagittal CT reformat image reveals a T9 spinal fracture dislocation. The patient had unequivocal clinical findings indicating spinal cord transection. What deficits will the patient incur?
choices: Loss of only sensory information below the lesion
Loss of only motor function below the lesion
questions.explanation: Complete transection at T9 spares upper limb function (supplied by C5-T1) but abolishes all motor, sensory, and autonomic function below the lesion, producing paraplegia along with fecal/urinary incontinence and loss of sacral parasympathetic outflow. Quadriplegia would require a cervical-level lesion; isolated incontinence or isolated sensory/motor loss all understate the global deficit produced by a complete cord transection.
keypoints: ⭐ Complete spinal cord transection causes loss of ALL motor, sensory, and autonomic function below the lesion
T9 transection spares upper limbs (C5-T1) but produces paraplegia, not quadriplegia
Sacral parasympathetic outflow (S2-4) loss causes bladder/bowel incontinence and sexual dysfunction
T10 dermatome landmark = umbilicus, useful for localizing thoracic spinal levels
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal CT reformat of the thoracic spine showing a T9 fracture-dislocation
questions.imageCaption: Sagittal CT showing T9 spinal fracture-dislocation

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman suffers intractable pain in her left forearm. Neurosurgical consultation leads to a decision to conduct a rhizotomy to relieve the condition. At which of the following locations is the rhizotomy best performed to relieve the patient's pain?
questions.explanation: The posterior (dorsal) roots are the only site where sensory (afferent) fibers are anatomically segregated from motor fibers, so selectively severing them relieves pain without causing motor deficits. Posterior primary rami carry sensation only from the back skin (not the forearm); spinal nerves and anterior primary rami carry mixed sensory and motor fibers, so cutting them would also cause motor loss; and anterior roots carry only motor fibers, which would not address the sensory pain.
keypoints: ⭐ Posterior (dorsal) roots are the only location with pure sensory fibers, ideal for selective rhizotomy
Anterior (ventral) roots contain only motor fibers
Spinal nerves and both primary rami contain mixed sensory + motor fibers
Posterior primary rami supply only back skin sensation — not the forearm

questions.stem: An 18-year-old soldier presents with shrapnel wounds in the lateral wall of his right chest. After recovery, his physical therapist observes that his scapula moves away from the thoracic wall when he leans on his right hand (winged scapula). Which of the following nerves is likely damaged?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve runs superficially on the lateral thoracic wall to innervate serratus anterior; its injury causes paralysis of serratus anterior and the classic winged scapula, in which the medial border and inferior angle lift away from the chest wall. The axillary nerve affects deltoid/teres minor (shoulder abduction/contour), the thoracodorsal nerve affects latissimus dorsi (arm extension/medial rotation), the dorsal scapular nerve affects rhomboids/levator scapulae (scapular retraction/elevation), and the suboccipital nerve is unrelated to the thorax.
keypoints: ⭐ Long thoracic nerve injury → serratus anterior paralysis → winged scapula
Long thoracic nerve's superficial course on the lateral thoracic wall makes it vulnerable to trauma/surgery
Serratus anterior normally rotates the scapula to allow full arm abduction above horizontal
Winging may take weeks to become apparent as the trapezius gradually stretches
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photo of a patient with winged scapula, showing the medial border of the scapula lifting away from the thoracic wall
questions.imageCaption: Winged right scapula due to long thoracic nerve injury

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman complains of weakness and loss of sensation in her legs. Radiological studies show bony spurs (osteophytes) narrowing the intervertebral foramina at levels T12-L3. Which of the following structures is most likely to be impinged in this condition?
choices: Posterior primary rami of spinal nerves
Anterior primary rami of spinal nerves
questions.explanation: Spinal (dorsal root) ganglia lie within the intervertebral foramina, alongside the merging roots, so foraminal stenosis from osteophytes directly compresses them (along with the roots and nerve). Primary rami (anterior and posterior) form distal to the foramen and would not be compressed there; sympathetic trunk ganglia lie outside the foramina along the vertebral column; and anterior rootlets are proximal to the foramen, closer to the spinal cord.
keypoints: ⭐ Spinal (dorsal root) ganglia are located within the intervertebral foramina — vulnerable to foraminal stenosis
Primary rami (anterior/posterior) form just distal to the foramen, outside the zone of compression
Sympathetic trunk ganglia lie lateral to the vertebral column, outside the foramina
Foraminal stenosis from osteophytes is a common cause of radiculopathy in older adults

questions.stem: A physician orders a lumbar puncture for his 43-year-old female patient, to be performed between the spinous processes of the L3 and L4 vertebrae. What is the best reason for performing the lumbar puncture at this location?
choices: The medullary cone ends at or above the L3 level
The subarachnoid space ends at the L3 level
The intervertebral foramina at L3-4 are large and easy to penetrate
No vertebral venous plexuses exist below the L3 level
The ligamenta flava are absent below the L3 level
questions.explanation: The medullary cone (conus medullaris), the spinal cord's tapered terminal end, normally lies within the T12-L3 vertebral levels, so inserting a needle below L3 avoids puncturing the spinal cord itself. The subarachnoid space actually extends well below L3 (to ~S2), providing the lumbar cistern of CSF used for the tap; the lumbar puncture is performed through the interlaminar space (not the intervertebral foramen); vertebral venous plexuses and the ligamentum flavum are present at all lumbar levels.
keypoints: ⭐ Lumbar puncture is performed below L3 (typically L3-4 or L4-5) to avoid the conus medullaris (ends ~L1-L2/L3)
Subarachnoid space extends to ~S2, forming the lumbar cistern — the actual site tapped for CSF
Needle passes through interlaminar space (not intervertebral foramen) and through the ligamentum flavum
Patient flexion (fetal position) widens the interlaminar spaces to ease needle passage

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the ER with severe back pain and lower limb weakness after falling off a 16-ft ladder and landing on his feet. The given midsagittal CT directs the physician toward making which of the following diagnoses?
choices: Burst fracture of T12 vertebral body
questions.explanation: Axial loading from a fall onto the feet classically produces a burst (compression) fracture of a vertebral body — here T12 — with a posteriorly displaced fragment compressing the conus medullaris; CT is the modality of choice for assessing bone injury. In a young patient, discs are typically stronger than bone (making herniation less likely than fracture), and the CT shows no evidence of foraminal/canal narrowing from degeneration (stenosis), anterior slippage at L5-S1, or abnormal lumbar curvature.
keypoints: ⭐ Axial loading (fall onto feet/head) → burst (compression) fracture of vertebral body
CT is optimal for bone injury; MRI is better for discs, cord, and ligaments
In young patients, vertebrae often fracture before discs herniate (discs are relatively strong)
Burst fracture fragments displaced posteriorly can compress the conus medullaris/cauda equina
questions.imageAlt: Midsagittal CT of the thoracolumbar spine showing a burst fracture of the T12 vertebral body
questions.imageCaption: Midsagittal CT showing T12 burst fracture with posterior fragment displacement

questions.stem: After several months of engaging in a vigorous exercise program, a 28-year-old woman experiences periodic pain and muscle spasms in her left upper limb. Examinations determine that she suffers a posterolateral herniation of the C5-6 intervertebral disc. Which of the following structures is this herniation most likely impinging?
choices: C7 posterior horn segment of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Using the cervical 'N+1' rule (because there are 8 cervical nerve pairs but only 7 cervical vertebrae, each numbered nerve exits above its like-numbered vertebra), a herniated C5-6 disc impinges the C6 nerve roots as they pass through the C5-6 foramen. C5 roots exit at the C4-5 level (above this disc); primary rami (anterior or posterior) form outside the vertebral canal/foramen and are not impinged by disc herniation; and the C7 spinal cord segment lies below and on the opposite side from the herniation site.
keypoints: ⭐ Cervical disc herniation rule: 'N+1' — the C(N)-(N+1) disc impinges the C(N+1) nerve root
8 cervical nerve pairs but only 7 cervical vertebrae — cervical nerves exit above their matched vertebra
In the lumbar spine, the rule works differently: nerve roots exit below their matched vertebra due to sharp downward angulation
Primary rami (structures outside the vertebral canal) are never directly impinged by disc herniation

questions.stem: During a head-on motor vehicle accident, the upper cervical vertebrae of a 34-year-old woman are flexed violently forward until her head impacts the steering wheel and is thrown into hyperextension and slight rotation. The given sagittal CT of her upper cervical vertebrae reveals which of the following diagnoses?
choices: Ruptured intervertebral disc between C1 and C2
No pathology is apparent on the CT scan
questions.explanation: This combination of flexion followed by hyperextension with slight rotation is the classic mechanism for a Type II dens (odontoid process) fracture, the most common odontoid fracture pattern, occurring at the base of the dens; the fragment here does not extend posteriorly into the spinal cord. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 (hangman fracture) results from pure hyperextension and involves the pars interarticularis (better seen on lateral X-ray), atlanto-axial subluxation requires transverse ligament rupture (not present here), and no disc exists between C1 and C2 so this diagnosis is anatomically impossible.
keypoints: ⭐ Type II odontoid (dens) fracture: ~60% of dens fractures, occurs at the base of the dens
Mechanism often involves combined flexion/extension/rotation forces
Hangman fracture (traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2) results from pure hyperextension, affecting the pars interarticularis
Steele's Rule of Thirds: atlas ring occupied 1/3 by dens, 1/3 by cord, 1/3 by protective space
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal CT of the upper cervical spine showing a fracture at the base of the dens (odontoid process) of C2
questions.imageCaption: Sagittal CT showing a Type II dens (odontoid process) fracture

questions.stem: As a result of multiple vertebral fractures incurred in an automobile crash, an 8-year-old girl suffers a series of torn posterior primary rami of spinal nerves C1-6. Which of the following muscles will be paralyzed as a result?
questions.explanation: Splenius capitis is an epimere-derived intrinsic (epaxial) back muscle innervated by posterior (dorsal) primary rami, so damage to C1-6 posterior rami would paralyze it. Trapezius is innervated by CN XI (not a myotome-derivative rami-supplied muscle), while latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae, and rhomboid major are hypomere-derived superficial back muscles innervated by anterior (ventral) primary rami, not posterior rami.
keypoints: ⭐ Splenius capitis/cervicis are epaxial (deep back) muscles supplied by posterior primary rami
Superficial 'extrinsic' back muscles (latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae) are hypaxial, supplied by anterior primary rami
Trapezius is supplied by CN XI (accessory nerve), independent of both rami
Deep/epaxial muscles derive from the epimere; superficial/hypaxial limb-related muscles derive from the hypomere

questions.stem: A 17-year-old gymnast grips a high bar with his arms outstretched and begins to pull himself straight upward to the level of the bar, as in doing a chin-up. Which of the following muscles is the prime agonist in this action?
questions.explanation: The latissimus dorsi, a large superficial extrinsic back muscle acting on the humerus, powerfully extends and medially rotates the arm to raise the trunk toward a fixed upper limb, making it the prime mover in chin-ups/climbing. Serratus posterior superior is a small accessory respiratory muscle, rhomboid major and levator scapulae stabilize/move the scapula rather than driving the pulling motion, and longissimus is a deep back extensor unattached to the upper limb.
keypoints: ⭐ Latissimus dorsi is the prime mover for pulling/climbing movements (extension + medial rotation of the arm)
Well-developed latissimus dorsi produces the classic 'V-taper' back shape in athletes
Rhomboids and levator scapulae act as synergists/stabilizers of the scapula during the movement
Longissimus is part of the erector spinae group, acting on the vertebral column, not the limb

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man presents with shingles on his anterolateral abdomen and umbilicus, caused by reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in sensory ganglia. Given the location of the rash, what ganglion is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: The umbilicus corresponds to the T10 dermatome, and because varicella zoster resides latent in sensory (not autonomic) ganglia, reactivation causing a rash at T10 implicates the spinal (dorsal root) ganglion of T10. Paravertebral, prevertebral, and lumbar ganglia are all autonomic (sympathetic) ganglia that do not harbor the latent virus responsible for shingles, and the L2 dermatome covers the anteromedial thigh, not the umbilicus.
keypoints: ⭐ T10 dermatome landmark = umbilicus; herpes zoster there implies T10 spinal (dorsal root) ganglion involvement
Varicella zoster remains latent specifically in sensory (dorsal root or cranial sensory) ganglia, not autonomic ganglia
Autonomic ganglia (paravertebral, prevertebral, lumbar) are not typical zoster reservoirs
Shingles rash classically follows a single dermatome distribution unilaterally
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photo of a unilateral vesicular shingles rash along the T10 dermatome on the anterolateral abdomen
questions.imageCaption: Herpes zoster (shingles) rash along the T10 dermatome

questions.stem: An anesthesiologist administers epidural anesthetic immediately lateral to the spinous processes of vertebrae L3 and L4 of a pregnant woman in labor. During this procedure, what would be the last ligament perforated by the needle in order to access the epidural space?
questions.explanation: Passing posterior-to-anterior, the needle traverses the supraspinous ligament, then the interspinous ligament, and finally the elastic-fiber-rich ligamentum flavum (often felt as a distinct 'pop') just before entering the epidural space. The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments lie anterior/posterior to the vertebral bodies (beyond the epidural space) and are not encountered, and the intertransverse ligament lies off the midline sagittal plane used for the approach.
keypoints: ⭐ Needle order for midline epidural: skin → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space
Ligamentum flavum's elastic fibers create palpable resistance and a 'pop' on penetration
Epidural space lies between the ligamentum flavum and the posterior longitudinal ligament/dura
Anterior/posterior longitudinal ligaments are not traversed in a standard posterior epidural approach

questions.stem: During a routine prenatal examination of a pregnant 16-year-old woman at 15 weeks of gestation, elevated maternal serum AFP levels were detected and confirmed by amniocentesis. A follow-up ultrasound reveals defects in the lower back of the fetus, with a cyst-like sac containing protruding neural tissue. Which of the following terms best describes this neural tube defect?
questions.explanation: A protruding cyst-like sac containing both meninges and spinal cord/nerve tissue is a meningomyelocele, the most common form of spina bifida cystica, typically associated with elevated maternal serum and amniotic AFP. A meningocele contains only meninges/CSF (no neural tissue) within its sac, spina bifida occulta shows no protrusion at all (and normal AFP), anencephaly is a cranial (not lumbar) defect, and rachischisis shows exposed neural tissue with no covering sac at all.
keypoints: ⭐ Meningomyelocele = protruding sac containing both meninges AND spinal cord/nerve tissue (most common spina bifida cystica)
Meningocele = sac contains only meninges/CSF, cord remains in normal position
Rachischisis (spina bifida with myeloschisis) = exposed neural tissue with no membranous covering at all
Elevated maternal serum/amniotic AFP is characteristic of open neural tube defects

questions.imageCaption: Prenatal ultrasound showing a meningomyelocele

questions.stem: A 25-year-old medical student feels a sharp pain in his lower back while helping move a piano. After 3 days, a comprehensive examination reveals a compression of the left side L3 spinal nerve. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this condition?
choices: The pedicles of L2 and L3 are compressed together
The pedicles of L3 and L4 are compressed together
The laminae of L2 and L3 are compressed together
The laminae of L3 and L4 are compressed together
The spinous processes of L3 and L4 are compressed together
questions.explanation: In the lumbar spine, each numbered spinal nerve exits through the intervertebral foramen formed by the pedicles of its own vertebra and the vertebra above it; thus the L3 nerve exits through the foramen bounded by the L2 and L3 pedicles, and compression of those pedicles narrows that foramen and impinges the L3 nerve. Compression of the L3-L4 pedicles would instead narrow the foramen through which the L4 nerve passes, and compression of laminae or spinous processes does not narrow the intervertebral foramen (it may even widen it via a lever-arm effect) and would not impinge a spinal nerve.
keypoints: ⭐ Lumbar spinal nerves exit the foramen BELOW their same-numbered vertebra (formed by pedicles of that vertebra and the one above)
L3 nerve exits through the L2-L3 intervertebral foramen
Foramina are bounded by pedicles, not laminae or spinous processes
Cervical spinal nerves instead exit ABOVE their same-numbered vertebra (due to the extra 8th cervical nerve)

questions.stem: A school nurse notices a 12-year-old girl's right scapula is more prominent than the left, her head is not centered directly over the pelvis, and her right hip is raised and more prominent. When the girl bends forward at the waist, the nurse observes asymmetry of the trunk. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
questions.explanation: Scoliosis is an abnormal lateral and rotational curvature of the spine that produces asymmetric shoulders/scapulae, uneven hips, and a trunk that is off-center from the pelvis, with asymmetry accentuated on forward bending (Adam's forward bend test) — classic for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in this age group. Lordosis and kyphosis are excessive curvatures in the sagittal (not lateral) plane, and osteoporosis/osteoarthritis are degenerative conditions of older individuals, not consistent with this presentation in a 12-year-old.
keypoints: ⭐ Scoliosis = lateral + rotational spinal curvature; classically screened via forward-bend test
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis has onset ages 10-18, most common in this demographic
Lordosis = excessive anterior concave curvature (normal in cervical/lumbar spine); kyphosis = excessive posterior convex curvature (normal in thoracic/sacral spine)
Curvatures <20° often need no treatment; >25° may require bracing

questions.stem: After moving heavy furniture, a 38-year-old man experiences lower back pain with tingling numbness radiating down his right lower limb to the lateral part of his foot and weakness standing on his toes. A T1-weighted MRI revealed an intervertebral disc herniation. Which of the following structures is most likely impinged by this disc herniation?
questions.explanation: Approximately 90% of disc herniations occur at L4-5 or L5-S1; using the lumbar 'N+1' rule, an L5-S1 herniation impinges the S1 nerve roots, consistent with lateral foot numbness and weak plantarflexion (toe-standing), both S1-mediated findings. L5 roots exit above this disc level (held against the L5 pedicle, above the L5-S1 disc) and would not be impinged here, and primary rami (anterior or posterior, at either level) lie outside the vertebral canal/foramen and are not directly impinged by disc herniation.
keypoints: ⭐ L5-S1 disc herniation ('N+1' rule) most often impinges the S1 nerve roots
S1 radiculopathy: weakness in plantarflexion (toe walking), numbness in lateral foot/sole
L5 radiculopathy (from L4-5 disc): weakness in dorsiflexion, numbness over dorsum of foot/big toe
~90% of lumbar disc herniations occur at L4-5 or L5-S1
