questions.imageCaption: Sagittal lumbar MRI showing L5-S1 disc herniation impinging the S1 nerve roots

questions.stem: A 24-year-old BMX rider fell from 20 ft and landed on his feet. A sagittal CT reveals a burst fracture of the L1 vertebral body with a posteriorly displaced fracture fragment compressing the medullary cone (conus medullaris). Which of the following spinal cord segments would most likely be impinged by the bone fragment in this injury?
questions.explanation: The conus medullaris (composed of the sacral and coccygeal spinal cord segments) typically ends around the L1-L2 vertebral level, so a burst fracture fragment at L1 compressing the conus would most likely impinge its lower (sacral) segments — S2 is the only sacral-level choice offered. T7, T9, T11, and L2 spinal cord segments all lie well above the conus medullaris/L1 fracture site and would not be affected by this specific injury.
keypoints: ⭐ 'Rule of 2': conus medullaris ends ~L2; subarachnoid space ends ~S2; filum terminale attaches ~Co2
Conus medullaris = sacral and coccygeal spinal cord segments compressed together at its tapered end
Spinal cord segment level does not equal vertebral level below the cervical region, due to differential growth
L1 burst fractures are a classic cause of conus medullaris syndrome

questions.stem: As a result of chronic stress associated with an intense high school weight-lifting program, a 15-year-old boy suffers an avulsion fracture of the greater tubercle of the humerus. In the ER, he displays difficulty initiating abduction of the upper limb. Which of the following muscles was involved in this fracture?
questions.explanation: The greater tubercle is the insertion site for supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor, but only supraspinatus initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction before the deltoid takes over, so its avulsion explains the inability to initiate abduction. The long head of biceps brachii runs through the intertubercular groove (not the greater tubercle) and its avulsion causes a biceps bulge, the long head of triceps attaches to the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, and subscapularis inserts on the lesser (not greater) tubercle.
keypoints: ⭐ Supraspinatus initiates the first ~15 degrees of shoulder abduction; deltoid continues the motion afterward
Greater tubercle = insertion for supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor (3 of the 4 rotator cuff muscles)
Lesser tubercle = insertion for subscapularis (the 4th rotator cuff muscle)
Infraspinatus and teres minor primarily produce external (lateral) rotation, not abduction initiation

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy comes to the emergency room after a hard fall onto the lateral aspect of his left shoulder. On physical examination, the distal end of the clavicle is prominent and distinctly palpable. Radiological findings confirm the diagnosis of a severe (grade 3) shoulder separation. Which of the following features is a component of this condition?
choices: Dislocated sternal end of the clavicle
questions.explanation: 'Shoulder separation' refers to dislocation of the acromioclavicular (AC) joint; in its most severe (grade 3) form, both the intrinsic AC ligament and the extrinsic coracoclavicular ligament tear, allowing the scapula to fall away from the clavicle and the distal clavicle to become prominent. The glenohumeral joint and its ligaments are uninvolved (this is an AC, not GH, injury), the sternoclavicular joint is rarely dislocated due to its intrinsic strength, and no clavicular fracture was found on imaging.
keypoints: ⭐ 'Shoulder separation' = acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury, not glenohumeral dislocation
Grade 3 separation = complete tear of both AC ligament and coracoclavicular ligament
Prominent, palpable distal clavicle is the classic exam finding
Sternoclavicular dislocation is rare due to strong ligamentous support; more often the clavicular epiphysis fractures in patients <25

questions.stem: An 18-year-old boy is cut severely on the lateral wall of his right chest during a knife fight. Following healing, his scapula moves away from the thoracic wall when he leans on his right hand (winged scapula, as in the given photo). Which of the following nerves is likely damaged?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve runs superficially along the lateral thoracic wall on serratus anterior, making it vulnerable to lacerations there; its injury paralyzes serratus anterior, producing the classic winged scapula and inability to abduct the arm above horizontal. The axillary nerve affects the deltoid/teres minor, the thoracodorsal nerve affects latissimus dorsi, the dorsal scapular nerve affects levator scapulae/rhomboids, and the suprascapular nerve affects supraspinatus/infraspinatus — none of which produce this classic winging sign.
keypoints: ⭐ Long thoracic nerve injury → serratus anterior paralysis → winged scapula
Long thoracic nerve's superficial course on the lateral thoracic wall makes it especially vulnerable to trauma/surgery
Serratus anterior normally rotates the scapula superiorly, enabling full arm abduction above horizontal
Contrast with trapezius (CN XI) winging, which produces a laterally displaced (not medially displaced) scapula
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photo of a winged right scapula, with the medial border and inferior angle lifted away from the thoracic wall
questions.imageCaption: Winged scapula due to long thoracic nerve injury

questions.stem: A dermatologist excised a substantial amount of tissue surrounding a malignant melanoma on the right side of the posterior neck of a 57-year-old man. After the procedure, the patient experienced difficulty elevating his right shoulder and lifting his right arm over his head. No sensory deficits were seen. What nerve was most likely damaged in this patient?
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve (CN XI) runs superficially through the posterior triangle of the neck en route to the trapezius, making it vulnerable during posterior neck surgery; its injury impairs scapular elevation and the lateral rotation of the scapula needed for abduction above 90 degrees, matching this patient's deficits with no sensory loss (CN XI is purely motor). The axillary, long thoracic, and thoracodorsal nerves arise more distally (in the axilla/arm), not the posterior neck, and the dorsal scapular nerve produces different deficits (scapular retraction/elevation via rhomboids/levator scapulae, but lies deeper and less exposed than CN XI in this region).
keypoints: ⭐ Accessory nerve (CN XI) runs superficially through the posterior triangle of the neck — vulnerable in neck surgery/biopsy
CN XI is purely motor to trapezius (and sternocleidomastoid) — explains absence of sensory deficit
Trapezius elevates the scapula and rotates it laterally to assist abduction above 90 degrees
Iatrogenic CN XI injury is a classically tested complication of posterior cervical lymph node biopsy

questions.stem: A 17-year-old male football player suffers a shoulder dislocation. After reduction, no fractures are seen on X-rays, but the patient displays weakness in abduction and external rotation at the shoulder, with loss of sensation at the superior and lateral aspects of the arm. What nerve was most likely damaged in this injury?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve, injured in roughly 1 in 7 shoulder dislocations, supplies the deltoid (abduction) and teres minor (assists external rotation) as well as cutaneous sensation over the superolateral arm — matching this patient's motor and sensory deficits exactly. The median and ulnar nerves have no motor branches proximal to the elbow and sensory distributions limited to the hand/wrist; the radial nerve affects elbow/wrist extension; and the musculocutaneous nerve affects elbow flexion/supination with lateral forearm (not arm) sensation.
keypoints: ⭐ Axillary nerve: motor to deltoid + teres minor; sensory to skin over the deltoid (superolateral arm)
Axillary nerve injury is a well-known complication of anterior shoulder (glenohumeral) dislocation
Deltoid loss → weak abduction; teres minor loss → weak external rotation (assisting infraspinatus)
'Regimental badge' sensory loss over the deltoid area is the classic exam sign of axillary nerve injury

questions.stem: A physician tests the myotatic biceps reflex as shown. A normal response of involuntary contraction of the biceps brachii muscle is noted. This reflex confirms the integrity of what nerve?
questions.explanation: The biceps reflex tests the musculocutaneous nerve (and its C5-C6 spinal segments of origin), which supplies motor innervation and proprioception to the biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis in the anterior arm. The axillary nerve supplies deltoid/teres minor, the median and ulnar nerves have no motor branches above the elbow, and the radial nerve supplies posterior (extensor) compartment muscles — none of which mediate this specific reflex.
keypoints: ⭐ Biceps reflex tests the musculocutaneous nerve and spinal segments C5-C6
Musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm: coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis
Deep tendon reflexes test both motor output and the sensory (proprioceptive) afferent limb of the reflex arc
Compare: triceps reflex tests the radial nerve (C7-C8); brachioradialis reflex tests the radial nerve (C5-C6)
questions.imageAlt: Photo of a physician testing the biceps myotatic reflex with a reflex hammer at the antecubital fossa
questions.imageCaption: Testing of the biceps reflex (musculocutaneous nerve, C5-C6)

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is stabbed multiple times in the back with a long, narrow-bladed letter-opener, with a puncture wound in the posterior axillary fold. The patient presents with weakness in extension, adduction, and medial rotation of his arm. Which of the following muscles is most likely cut in this injury?
questions.explanation: The latissimus dorsi, together with teres major, forms the palpable posterior axillary fold and the posterior wall of the axilla; it produces extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm, matching this patient's deficits exactly. Pectoralis minor and serratus anterior form the anterior and medial axillary walls respectively (not the posterior fold), levator scapulae is unrelated to the axilla or arm rotation, and teres minor is a lateral (not medial) rotator.
keypoints: ⭐ Posterior axillary fold = latissimus dorsi + teres major; forms the posterior wall of the axilla
Latissimus dorsi actions: extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm
Anterior axillary fold = pectoralis major; anterior axillary wall also includes pectoralis minor
Medial axillary wall = serratus anterior + thoracic wall; lateral wall = intertubercular groove of humerus

questions.stem: Physical examination of a 45-year-old man who had been stabbed in the back of the shoulder shows a deep wound penetrating into the quadrangular space of the shoulder, causing bleeding from the severed blood vessels there. Which of the following neural structures is most likely damaged as well?
choices: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm
questions.explanation: The quadrangular space (bounded by teres major, teres minor, the long head of triceps, and the surgical neck of the humerus) transmits the posterior circumflex humeral vessels together with the axillary nerve, so injury here damages the axillary nerve. The musculocutaneous nerve and lateral cord lie in the axilla proper (not the quadrangular space), the radial nerve instead travels through the adjacent triangular interval/radial groove, and the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm arises from the medial cord, unrelated to this space.
keypoints: ⭐ Quadrangular space contents: axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral vessels
Quadrangular space boundaries: teres minor (superior), teres major (inferior), long head of triceps (medial), surgical neck of humerus (lateral)
Radial nerve instead passes through the triangular interval and radial (spiral) groove of the humerus
Axillary nerve injury here produces deltoid/teres minor weakness and superolateral arm sensory loss

questions.stem: Lateral rotation of the arm is an important mechanical component of "bringing the arm back" when preparing to throw an object. What muscle acts to produce lateral rotation of the arm?
questions.explanation: Teres minor, along with infraspinatus, lies across the posterior aspect of the glenohumeral joint and is a primary external (lateral) rotator of the arm, assisted by the posterior deltoid fibers. Supraspinatus initiates abduction (not rotation); teres major, latissimus dorsi, and subscapularis all cross the joint posterior-to-anterior and instead produce medial (internal) rotation along with adduction/extension.
keypoints: ⭐ Lateral (external) rotators of the arm: infraspinatus and teres minor (posterior rotator cuff), assisted by posterior deltoid
Medial (internal) rotators: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, anterior deltoid
Mnemonic: 'teres minor = minor (lateral)' rotator vs. 'teres major = major (medial)' rotator direction
Rotator cuff muscles (SItS): Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, teres minor, Subscapularis

questions.stem: The given X-ray reveals a fracture of the proximal humerus (surgical neck), indicated by the black arrow. Given the location of the fracture, what artery is most likely damaged in this patient?
questions.explanation: The posterior circumflex humeral artery travels with the axillary nerve directly against the posterior aspect of the surgical neck of the humerus as they pass into the quadrangular space, making both structures vulnerable to surgical neck fractures. The brachial artery runs down the midline of the arm (away from the surgical neck), the deep brachial artery and radial nerve are instead endangered by midshaft/radial groove fractures, the subscapular artery runs along the scapula's axillary border, and the superior ulnar collateral artery is at risk with medial epicondyle fractures.
keypoints: ⭐ Surgical neck of humerus fracture endangers the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Midshaft/radial groove fracture instead endangers the radial nerve and profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery
Surgical neck fractures are the most common proximal humeral fractures, especially in elderly patients (osteoporotic bone)
Medial epicondyle fractures risk the ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
questions.imageAlt: AP X-ray of the proximal humerus with an arrow indicating a fracture of the surgical neck
questions.imageCaption: Surgical neck fracture of the humerus, endangering the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery

questions.stem: A right-handed 21-year-old college student develops pain in his right shoulder after 2 weeks of a construction job regularly lifting heavy materials overhead. During physical examination, the patient experiences sharp pain in the range of 80 to 150 degrees of abduction at the glenohumeral joint. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic shoulder impingement syndrome, in which the supraspinatus tendon is compressed beneath the acromion during a mid-range 'painful arc' of abduction (80-150 degrees), producing supraspinatus tendonitis from repetitive overhead activity. Infraspinatus tendonitis instead causes pain with resisted external rotation; AC arthritis and degenerative shoulder arthritis are unlikely given this patient's young age and short symptom duration; and a broken clavicle would cause constant pain following a discrete trauma, not activity-related arc pain.
keypoints: ⭐ Painful arc (80-150° abduction) = classic sign of supraspinatus tendonitis/shoulder impingement syndrome
Caused by repetitive overhead activity compressing the supraspinatus tendon beneath the acromion
Infraspinatus tendonitis instead presents with pain on resisted external rotation, not an abduction arc
Degenerative joint conditions (AC arthritis, glenohumeral osteoarthritis) are atypical in young, otherwise healthy patients

questions.stem: The traditional radical mastectomy includes removal of the pectoralis major muscle. Which of the following movements is most affected postoperatively by this surgical procedure?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major's primary actions are adduction, flexion, and medial rotation of the arm, so its removal in a radical (Halsted) mastectomy most directly weakens adduction (though other muscles like subscapularis and latissimus dorsi partially compensate). Abduction is produced by supraspinatus/deltoid/serratus anterior, extension mainly by latissimus dorsi and posterior deltoid, and lateral rotation by infraspinatus/teres minor/posterior deltoid — all antagonists to, and unaffected by loss of, the pectoralis major.
keypoints: ⭐ Pectoralis major actions: adduction, flexion, and medial rotation of the arm
Radical (Halsted) mastectomy removes both pectoralis major and pectoralis minor along with breast tissue
Neighboring muscles (subscapularis, latissimus dorsi, anterior deltoid) partially compensate for lost adduction/medial rotation
Modified radical mastectomy, more common today, spares the pectoralis major

questions.stem: Following a radical mastectomy procedure, a surgeon plans to conduct a breast reconstruction utilizing a latissimus dorsi muscle flap. What nerve will the surgeon need to keep intact during the surgical dissection of the chest wall to prevent atrophy of the muscle flap?
questions.explanation: The latissimus dorsi is innervated by the thoracodorsal (middle subscapular) nerve, a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, so preserving this nerve is essential to keep the muscle flap viable and prevent denervation atrophy. The long thoracic nerve instead supplies serratus anterior, the intercostobrachial nerve is purely sensory to the medial arm, the medial pectoral nerve supplies the (already removed) pectoralis muscles, and the axillary nerve supplies deltoid/teres minor — none innervate latissimus dorsi.
keypoints: ⭐ Thoracodorsal nerve (middle subscapular nerve) is the motor supply to latissimus dorsi
Thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, running with the thoracodorsal artery
Preserving the neurovascular pedicle (nerve + vessels) is essential for flap viability in reconstructive surgery
Long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior) and medial pectoral nerve (pectoralis muscles) are different nerves relevant to breast/axillary surgery
